Authors: Wittwer, J. & Renkl, A.
Title: Why Instructional Explanations Often Do Not Work: A Framework for Understanding the Effectiveness of Instructional Explanations
Key_Finding: Explanations systematically fail for three reasons: not adapted to learner prior knowledge, learners process them passively, and instructors misjudge what learners already know. Explanations paired with self-explanation prompts outperform monologue delivery.
Population: Theoretical framework synthesizing tutoring, cooperative learning, and multimedia studies

Authors: Renkl, A.
Title: Toward an Instructionally Oriented Theory of Example-Based Learning
Key_Finding: Start with complete demonstrations, then progressively fade worked steps as competence develops (fading principle); use multiple examples varying surface features; explicitly prompt self-explanation at each step.
Population: Theoretical integration across worked examples, observational learning, and analogical reasoning research

Authors: Barbieri, C. A., Miller-Cotto, D., Clerjuste, S. N., & Chawla, K.
Title: A Meta-analysis of the Worked Examples Effect on Mathematics Performance
Key_Finding: Worked examples outperform problem-solving alone across 55 studies and 181 effect sizes. Pairing with self-explanation prompts did NOT consistently amplify the effect (negative moderator — surprising).
Population: Elementary through postsecondary math students

Authors: Tullis, J. G. & Feder, B.
Title: The 'curse of knowledge' when predicting others' knowledge
Key_Finding: When experts study facts before estimating what novices know, their growing knowledge impairs both calibration and resolution of estimates. Estimators lack diagnostic cues about others' knowledge.
Population: Undergraduate participants across four experiments using trivia questions

Authors: Merrill, M. D.
Title: First Principles of Instruction
Key_Finding: Five prescriptive principles common to ALL effective instruction: real-world problems, activation, demonstration, application, integration. Functions as a universal litmus test for any course design regardless of ID model used.
Population: Theoretical synthesis comparing major ID theories (~4000 citations)

Authors: Means, B., Toyama, Y., Murphy, R., & Baki, M.
Title: The Effectiveness of Online and Blended Learning: A Meta-Analysis of the Empirical Literature
Key_Finding: Online conditions outperformed face-to-face (d=+0.20) and blended learning showed the largest advantage (d=+0.35). But blended advantage was confounded with additional learning time — it's the design quality, not the delivery medium, that determines effectiveness.
Effect_Size: d=+0.20 online vs F2F; d=+0.35 blended vs F2F
Population: 51 rigorous studies; mostly higher education and medical training adults

Authors: Doo, M. Y. & Zhu, M.
Title: A Meta-analysis of Effects of Self-Directed Learning in Online Learning Environments
Key_Finding: Self-monitoring and motivation showed significantly larger effects on learning achievement than self-management. Helping learners set goals and monitor progress matters more than giving them scheduling tools.
Population: 152 samples from 43 studies in online learning environments across age groups

Authors: Guo, P. J., Kim, J., & Rubin, R.
Title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
Journal: Proceedings of the First ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S '14)
Key_Finding: Videos ≤6 minutes maintained near-100% engagement; engagement drops sharply after that threshold. Informal talking-head outperformed high-production studio recordings. Khan-style tablet drawing more engaging than PowerPoint slides.
Population: 6.9 million video watching sessions across edX MOOCs; 862 videos; ~128K students

Authors: Schneider, S., Beege, M., Nebel, S., & Rey, G. D.
Title: A Meta-analysis of How Signaling Affects Learning with Media
Key_Finding: Visual signals (highlights, arrows, color-coding) produce medium effects on retention and transfer. Prior knowledge was NOT a moderator — signaling benefits both novices and experts, contradicting expertise reversal predictions.
Population: 103 studies; 12201 participants; mostly lab-based multimedia studies

Authors: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Sanders, T., Parker, P. D., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C.
Title: Multimedia Design for Learning: An Overview of Reviews With Meta-Meta-Analysis
Key_Finding: 11 design principles with significant positive effects on learning. Strongest effects for procedural content (g=0.73) and conceptual content (g=0.62) — directly relevant to tech tutorials which are predominantly procedural.
Effect_Size: Overall g≈0.51; procedural g=0.73; conceptual g=0.62
Population: 29 systematic reviews; 1189 studies; 78177 participants

Authors: Beege, M., Schroeder, N. L., Heidig, S., Rey, G. D., & Schneider, S.
Title: The Instructor Presence Effect and Its Moderators in Instructional Video: A Series of Meta-Analyses
Key_Finding: Visible instructor produces a small but significant positive effect on retention but NO effect on transfer. Counter to the 'distraction' hypothesis, instructor presence REDUCED extraneous cognitive load. Smaller PIP format less distracting than large instructor images.
Effect_Size: Small positive on retention; null on transfer
Population: 35 studies; 6339 participants over 27 years of research

Authors: Ploetzner, R.
Title: The Effectiveness of Enhanced Interaction Features in Educational Videos: A Meta-Analysis
Key_Finding: Videos with enhanced interaction features (embedded questions, quizzes, self-explanation prompts) outperform passive viewing. Navigation features alone are insufficient — active processing prompts are necessary to break passive viewing patterns.
Population: 17 studies across educational video contexts

Authors: Wisniewski, B., Zierer, K., & Hattie, J.
Title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
Key_Finding: High-information feedback (explaining WHY errors occurred) yielded d=0.99 while low-information feedback (praise, rewards, punishment) yielded only d=0.14. Feedback type matters 7x more than its mere presence.
Effect_Size: d=0.48 overall; d=0.99 high-info; d=0.14 low-info
Population: 435 studies; 994 effect sizes; N>61000 learners across educational levels

Authors: Van der Kleij, F. M., Feskens, R. C. W., & Eggen, T. J. H. M.
Title: Effects of Feedback in a Computer-Based Learning Environment on Students' Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
Key_Finding: Clear hierarchy: elaborated feedback (d=0.49) >> knowledge of correct response (d=0.32) >> knowledge of results only (d=0.05). Simple right/wrong quiz feedback is almost worthless in digital learning environments.
Effect_Size: d=0.49 elaborated; d=0.32 KCR; d=0.05 KR only
Population: 40 studies; 70 effect sizes in computer-based learning environments

Authors: Brummer, L., de Boer, H., Mouw, J. M., & Strijbos, J.-W.
Title: A Meta-analysis of the Effects of Context, Content, and Task Factors of Digitally Delivered Instructional Feedback on Learning Performance
Key_Finding: Process-focused feedback emerged as particularly effective in digital environments. Learner control over feedback timing and format significantly influenced outcomes — especially relevant for self-paced contexts.
Population: 116 interventions across ages and disciplines

Authors: van Merriënboer, J. J. G., Clark, R. E., & de Croock, M. B. M.
Title: Blueprints for Complex Learning: The 4C/ID-Model
Key_Finding: Whole-task sequencing with scaffolding (worked examples → guided practice → independent practice) within task classes of increasing complexity produces better transfer than part-task approaches. Addresses compartmentalization, fragmentation, and the transfer paradox.
Population: Framework validated primarily in medical/healthcare education

Authors: Chen, Z., Liu, M., & Zhou, R.
Title: The More the Better? How Excessive Content and Online Interaction Hinder the Learning Effectiveness of High-Quality MOOCs
Key_Finding: Content richness has a curvilinear relationship with effectiveness: more content INCREASES dropout rates and DECREASES pass rates, especially for high-quality courses. Excessive online interaction similarly reduces pass rates.
Population: 8602 courses on a Chinese MOOC platform (Zhihuishu); observational design

Authors: Wigfield, A. & Eccles, J. S.
Title: Expectancy-Value Theory of Achievement Motivation
Key_Finding: Learners' choices, persistence, and performance are jointly determined by expectations of success AND subjective task value (attainment, intrinsic, utility, and cost). Directly translates into framework for writing learning objectives and module introductions.
Population: Original empirical work with children in academic settings; requires adaptation for adult contexts

Authors: Ryan, R. M. & Deci, E. L.
Title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation from a Self-Determination Theory Perspective: Definitions, Theory, Practices, and Future Directions
Key_Finding: Autonomy-supportive teaching strategies consistently enhance autonomous motivation, engagement, and adjustment across educational levels and cultures. The internalization continuum is crucial: help learners see personal value so extrinsic goals become self-endorsed.
Population: Comprehensive 20-year review across educational levels and cultures; discusses digital and self-paced contexts as emerging areas

Authors: Howard, J. L., Slemp, G. R., & Wang, X.
Title: Need Support and Need Thwarting: A Meta-Analysis of Autonomy, Competence, and Relatedness Supportive and Thwarting Behaviors in Student Populations
Key_Finding: Competence need satisfaction correlated positively with student performance and engagement. Supportive teacher behaviors correlated positively with desired student outcomes. Need-thwarting behaviors showed the opposite pattern. N=388912 across 637 samples.
Population: Primary school through university students in educational contexts

Authors: Berliner, D. C.
Title: Describing the Behavior and Documenting the Accomplishments of Expert Teachers
Key_Finding: Five-stage teaching expertise progression: Novice → Advanced Beginner → Competent → Proficient → Expert. Expertise is context-dependent — changing subject or audience temporarily reduces expertise. The 5-7+ year timeline provides realistic expectations.
Population: Theoretical model adapted from Dreyfus framework; based on K-12 teacher studies

Authors: Anderson, J. & Taner, G.
Title: Building the Expert Teacher Prototype: A Metasummary of Teacher Expertise Studies in Primary and Secondary Education
Key_Finding: Expert teachers reflect extensively and critically on practice, continuously learn, display flexibility, and build strong learner knowledge. Certain desirable practices like metacognitive instruction remain underdeveloped at ALL career stages — they require deliberate cultivation.
Population: 106 empirical studies; 16 countries; 1124 expert teachers; exclusively K-12
